title: McKinsey projects $769B AI infrastructure spend in 2026 as grid backlogs grow
subtitle: The consultancy's Technology Trends Outlook 2026 pegs AI infrastructure investment at more than five times the 2025 level, with 2,500 GW stuck in grid interconnect queues.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: McKinsey's Technology Trends Outlook 2026, summarized today in coverage by The Tribune and other outlets citing ANI and Times of Oman, projects that global investment in AI infrastructure and model architectures will reach roughly $769 billion in 2026. That figure is more than fivefold the $145 billion McKinsey attributes to 2025, and the firm says $384 billion of it was already committed in the first half of this year. The report compounds earlier McKinsey work that had put total data-center capital needs at about $6.7 trillion through 2030.

The numbers come with a caveat the report hammers on: dollars committed are not watts delivered. McKinsey flags energy shortages, specialized-talent gaps, and grid interconnect backlogs as the three constraints most likely to compress actual deployment below the headline investment. The firm's working figure for the interconnect queue is more than 2,500 gigawatts of generation and storage worldwide waiting for utility hook-up — a backlog measured in years, not months, in most major markets.

This matters because the AI capex cycle has been running on an implicit assumption that chips are the binding constraint. If the binding constraint is instead permitting, substations, transformers, and transmission lines, the political economy of the buildout shifts. State utility commissions, interconnection queue reform, and local land-use boards start to decide which labs get to train frontier models in 2027 and which don't. Nvidia's TSMC supply ramp is irrelevant to a project that can't get power until 2029.

For learners: when someone quotes an AI infrastructure number in the trillions, ask three follow-ups — over what period, measured in what (capex, revenue, GDP contribution), and sourced from whom. McKinsey's number is a 2026-only capex projection with explicit downside caveats; it is not the same thing as the $7-trillion-by-2030 figure that gets quoted interchangeably in press coverage. Learning to pull apart those three variables will keep you out of a lot of bad arguments.
